system:
You judge a requirements contract. A model interviewed the future users of a service and derived a contract from what they told it. You compare that contract with the reference requirements of the same service.

=== REFERENCE REQUIREMENTS (read-only) ===
BR-01: The service serves several independent operating companies at once. The staff of one operating company can never see or change another operating company's drones, models, sites, charging pads, jobs or flights, or their history.

BR-02: The airspace picture (the corridors between sites, the zones that group them, the prohibited zones and the closures) is one and the same for every company, and every company's staff can see all of it.

BR-03: Every member of staff acts in one of three roles: fleet technician or dispatcher at an operating company, or the airspace desk at the platform company. Each action of the service can be taken only by the role these requirements give it to.

BR-04: The airspace desk cannot see any one company's drones, jobs or flights.

BR-05: A fleet technician can add a drone to their company's fleet, stating its model. For each model the service holds how much it can carry, how far it can fly on a full battery, which sensors it carries, and which charging connector it uses.

BR-06: Each drone has a home site, one of its company's sites.

BR-07: A fleet technician can retire a drone. A retired drone stays in its company's history and is never again given a flight or sent to charge.

BR-08: A fleet technician can take a drone out of service for repair and put it back into service. A drone out of service cannot be given a flight.

BR-09: A fleet technician can set up a charging pad at one of their company's sites, stating its connector type.

BR-10: A charging pad is used only by drones of the company that owns it.

BR-11: A fleet technician can send a drone to charge. The service sends it only to a pad whose connector type is the one the drone's model uses, and refuses otherwise.

BR-12: The service keeps, for each drone, a record of when it was taken out of service, repaired or serviced, and put back, and by whom, so that its company can show a regulator how the drone has been looked after.

BR-13: A dispatcher can record a delivery job: a load to be carried from one site to another.

BR-14: A dispatcher can record an inspection job: the sensors it needs and a list of points to visit in a set order, ending back where it started.

BR-15: A dispatcher plans a flight for a job by choosing the drone and the way, a chain of corridors between named sites.

BR-16: The service never chooses a drone or a way for a flight, and never puts one in place of the dispatcher's choice.

BR-17: On a dispatcher's request, the service shows which of their company's drones could get to where a job starts.

BR-18: A flight leaves only after a dispatcher has signed it off; nothing but a dispatcher's own action signs a flight off.

BR-19: A dispatcher can call off a flight.

BR-20: The service refuses to sign off a flight whose drone cannot do the job: a load heavier than its model can carry, a way longer than its model can fly, or, for an inspection, a sensor the job needs that its model does not carry.

BR-21: The service refuses to sign off a flight whose way passes through a zone where flying is prohibited, or through a closure in force at any time during the flight.

BR-22: The service does not let more drones take off or land at a site at the same time than the site has places for.

BR-23: When dispatchers planning at the same time sign off flights that would use the same drone at overlapping times, only one sign-off succeeds, and the others are told why they failed.

BR-24: When it judges whether a drone can fly a way, the service does not count on the full range of a full battery, since batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned.

BR-25: The service accepts reports from people and devices outside the company that a flight's load is ready, that its drone has reached a point of its job, and that it has arrived, and it records each against the flight.

BR-26: A report that arrives more than once is applied once.

BR-27: A report that arrives late or out of order never undoes a later one: a flight's state follows the order in which things happened, not the order in which the reports arrived.

BR-28: When a report a flight is waiting for does not come in time, such as its arrival, the service flags the flight to the dispatchers of its company, since nobody watches every drone.

BR-29: A drone that restarts in flight and carries on stays on the same flight, and its reports after the restart count for that flight.

BR-30: The airspace desk can record the corridors between named sites, the zones that group them, and the zones where the authorities prohibit flying.

BR-31: The airspace desk can enter a planned closure, with a start and an end time, and a sudden closure, which applies at once. It can amend a closure, for example by widening its area or moving its end time, and the amendment applies from the moment it is entered.

BR-32: When a closure is entered or amended, the service tells each company's dispatchers which of their flights it affects, including flights already in the air, and tells no company about another's flights.

BR-33: The service does not itself call off, reroute or change a flight because of a closure; that is the dispatcher's decision.

BR-34: When a closure is entered, the airspace desk sees how much disruption it caused across the customers, as totals that name no company and show no company's flights.

BR-35: The service can be restarted, or crash, while drones are flying, and afterwards carries on from where it was: nothing it had recorded is lost or applied twice.

BR-36: An instruction the service sends to a drone or to charging equipment takes effect once, even when it gets through twice or the service sends it again because it cannot tell whether the first attempt arrived.

BR-37: The service tells each company's own systems what happens to that company's drones and jobs, and nothing about any other company's.

BR-38: The service offers no way to steer a drone.
=== END OF REFERENCE REQUIREMENTS ===

The names in the reference that look like `name` stand for these values:
(none)

=== OUT OF SCOPE: things the users said they do not want ===
- Management or analytical reports, exports, and dashboards.
- Login through an external identity provider.
- i18n.
- Compliance with any regulation, or a compliance audit. Regulations are cited as provenance only (`domain-profile.md` §9).
- Data retention and erasure: no retention schedule, deletion on request, or pseudonymisation of history.
- Backups.
- High availability or multi-node deployment.
- User accounts, sign-up, passwords, or user management. Staff identities are issued outside the system; each request carries a signed token (D-23).
- Notifying people by e-mail, text message, or phone. Domain events go only to the event webhook (D-18).
- Route planning or automatic choice of a drone. The system validates the dispatcher's choice and never makes it (D-33).
- Remote piloting or real-time flight control. Flight control is on the drone (`domain-profile.md` §2).
- Weather data or forecasts.
- Billing, invoicing, or pricing of deliveries and inspections.
- Onboarding of new operating companies or management of tenants through the system.
=== TECHNICAL ADDITIONS: never stated by the users, and not counted against a contract ===
- Autoscaling.
- A second-level cache.
- A message broker, queue, or coordinator. Every boundary is HTTP (`domain-profile.md` §3).
- Geometric or geospatial computation. Position is a location or a corridor; coordinates, if present, are descriptive (`domain-profile.md` §4, §6).
- Throughput or latency at the declared scale. Scale is data context (`domain-profile.md` §7); the harness does not apply fleet-scale load during functional gates.
=== END OF LISTS ===

You receive the contract: a list of items, each with an id and a requirement.

For each reference requirement, decide how the contract as a whole covers it:

- covered: the items, together, state every obligation of the requirement — every rule, condition, exception, value and outcome it gives. Wording, order, the words chosen for states and roles, and whether a value is given by its name or by its number do not matter; meaning does.
- partial: the items state at least one of its obligations and leave out at least one other.
- missing: no item states any of its obligations.

An item states an obligation only when it says what the service must do, or must not do, in a case the requirement covers. A general wish, such as that the service be reliable, states none. An item that says the opposite of an obligation does not state it. A requirement that only names another one, or a value another one defines, does not take over that other requirement's obligations.

For each item of the contract, decide its class:

- reference: it states one or more obligations of the reference requirements; name each requirement it states obligations of.
- user_visible: it asks for something on the out-of-scope list.
- technical: it asks for something on the list of technical additions.
- other: none of these — it asks for something no reference requirement asks for, or states nothing checkable.

A contract with no items covers nothing.

Reply with JSON only: an object with two keys. "requirements" is a list with exactly one entry for every reference requirement, in the reference's order; each entry has "id", the requirement's id, "coverage", one of "covered", "partial" or "missing", and "items", the ids of the items that state its obligations (an empty list when it is missing). "items" is a list with exactly one entry for every item of the contract, in the contract's order; each entry has "id", the item's id, "class", one of "reference", "user_visible", "technical" or "other", and "requirements", the ids of the reference requirements it states obligations of (an empty list unless its class is "reference").

messages.content:
The contract has 53 items:

- id: DR-01
  requirement: The service must keep each customer company's drones, charging pads, flights, sites and problems separate. A user from one company must never be able to see or change those of another company.
- id: DR-02
  requirement: The service must show the same airspace information (corridors, zones, prohibited zones and closures) to every customer company, with no company-specific version.
- id: DR-03
  requirement: It must be possible to add a new customer company to the service without changing or exposing the data of the companies already using it. The current customers are a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm and a hospital logistics firm, and others are expected to join.
- id: DR-04
  requirement: The service must work for a company with a few hundred drones of several models and manufacturers and a few dozen charging pads.
- id: DR-05
  requirement: A technician must be able to add a new drone to their company's fleet. The service must record its model, manufacturer, payload capacity, flight range on a full battery, sensors carried and charging connector type.
- id: DR-06
  requirement: A technician must be able to take a drone of their company out of service for repair and later put it back into service. The service must show at any time whether each drone is in service or out of service.
- id: DR-07
  requirement: A technician must be able to retire a drone. A retired drone must no longer be offered for flights or charging, but what was recorded about it must remain viewable.
- id: DR-08
  requirement: The service must not accept a sign-off for a flight whose drone is out of service or retired.
- id: DR-09
  requirement: When a drone on a flight that has not yet left is taken out of service or retired, the service must show this to the dispatcher on that flight. It must not replace the drone itself.
- id: DR-10
  requirement: The service must let a technician record each repair and each servicing carried out on a drone, with what was done and when. The company does this work itself.
- id: DR-11
  requirement: The service must show, for any single drone of the company, the full history of its repairs, servicing, removals from service, returns to service and retirement, so the company can show a regulator how that drone has been looked after.
- id: DR-12
  requirement: A technician must be able to set up a charging pad at one of their own company's sites. The service must record which site it is at and which connector type it has.
- id: DR-13
  requirement: A company's charging pad must only ever be usable for that company's drones. The service must never offer, show or assign it to another company.
- id: DR-14
  requirement: A technician must be able to send a drone to charge at a chosen pad of their company.
- id: DR-15
  requirement: The service must refuse to send a drone to a charging pad whose connector type differs from the drone's, because connector types are not interchangeable.
- id: DR-16
  requirement: The service must let a technician send a drone to charge at any moment, not only at times planned in advance, because batteries drain faster than planned in cold and wind.
- id: DR-17
  requirement: Every instruction the service sends to charging equipment must have the same effect whether the equipment receives it once or more than once. A duplicate delivery must not start a second action or undo the first.
- id: DR-18
  requirement: When the service has not received confirmation that an instruction reached the charging equipment, it must show that instruction as unconfirmed, not as done or failed. It must allow the instruction to be sent again, including after a restart or crash.
- id: DR-19
  requirement: A dispatcher must be able to plan a flight by choosing one drone from their own company's fleet and a way made up of corridors between named sites from the shared airspace picture.
- id: DR-20
  requirement: When a dispatcher is choosing a drone, the service must show each drone's payload capacity, flight range on a full battery, sensors carried and whether it is in service.
- id: DR-21
  requirement: The service must never choose, pre-select, suggest as a default, or change the drone or the way of a flight. This holds in every case, including when a closure affects the flight, when the drone goes out of service, and after a restart or crash.
- id: DR-22
  requirement: The service must record, for every flight, which dispatcher is the licensed person responsible for it, and must show this on the flight.
- id: DR-23
  requirement: The service must not show or treat a flight as having left unless a dispatcher has signed it off beforehand. For each sign-off it must record who signed, when, and for which drone and way.
- id: DR-24
  requirement: Only a dispatcher of the company that owns a flight may sign it off. Technicians, the airspace desk and users of other companies must not be able to.
- id: DR-25
  requirement: If the drone or the way of a flight is changed after sign-off and before the flight leaves, the earlier sign-off must no longer count. The flight must need a new sign-off for the new choice.
- id: DR-26
  requirement: A dispatcher must be able to call off any flight of their company that has not yet finished. The service must record who called it off and when, and show the flight as called off from then on.
- id: DR-27
  requirement: The airspace desk must be able to record and change the shared network of flight corridors between named sites and the zones that group those corridors.
- id: DR-28
  requirement: The airspace desk must be able to mark zones where the authorities prohibit flying. The service must show these as prohibited to all companies.
- id: DR-29
  requirement: Only the airspace desk may change corridors, zones, prohibited zones and closures. Users of customer companies must be able to view them but not change them.
- id: DR-30
  requirement: The airspace desk must be able to enter a planned closure with the area closed, a start time and an end time. The service must treat it as in force from the start time to the end time.
- id: DR-31
  requirement: The airspace desk must be able to enter a sudden closure. It must be in force from the moment it is entered, without a future start time being required.
- id: DR-32
  requirement: The airspace desk must be able to amend an existing closure, at least by widening its area and by moving its end time, as often as needed during the day. From the moment of the amendment every user must see the amended closure and not the old one.
- id: DR-33
  requirement: When a closure is entered, comes into force or is amended, the service must show each company's dispatchers which of their own company's flights have a way through the closed area during the closure. This covers flights not yet left and flights already in the air. It must not show them other companies' flights.
- id: DR-34
  requirement: When a dispatcher is about to sign off a flight, the service must show any prohibited zone or closure that covers part of the flight's way. The decision remains the dispatcher's.
- id: DR-35
  requirement: For each closure entered, the service must show the airspace desk how much disruption it caused across customers. At a minimum this is the total number of flights, across all companies, whose way passed through the closed area while the closure was in force, updated when the closure is amended.
- id: DR-36
  requirement: The service must record, for each site, how many drones can take off and land there at the same time. It must show a dispatcher when a flight they are planning would exceed that number at its departure or arrival site, without revealing another company's flights.
- id: DR-37
  requirement: The service must run on a single server.
- id: DR-38
  requirement: It must be possible to update and restart the service during working hours while flights are in progress, without first waiting for all drones to land.
- id: DR-39
  requirement: After a restart or crash, the service must be usable again within a few minutes, the length of interruption the companies and the airspace desk said they accept.
- id: DR-40
  requirement: After a restart or crash, everything the service had accepted before the interruption must still be present and unchanged. This covers drones and their status, service histories, pads, flights, sign-offs, call-offs, corridors, zones, closures and amendments.
- id: DR-41
  requirement: A restart or crash must not itself change any flight. Flights that were in the air must still be shown as in the air, signed-off flights must remain signed off, and no flight may be called off, reassigned or re-planned by the service because of the interruption.
- id: DR-42
  requirement: If a planned closure's start or end time passes while the service is stopped, the service must show the closure correctly as in force or ended as soon as it is running again.
- id: DR-43
  requirement: The service must not fly or steer drones or send flight commands to them. Drones fly on their own autopilots under supervision by people on the ground.
- id: DR-44
  requirement: The service must not send alerts to staff by e-mail, text message or phone. Anything it needs to tell users must be shown inside the service.
- id: DR-45
  requirement: The service must not include management or analytical reports, exports, or dashboards beyond what is needed for day-to-day operations.
- id: DR-46
  requirement: The service must not offer login through customers' own corporate identity systems.
- id: DR-47
  requirement: The service must not hold its own user accounts and passwords.
- id: DR-48
  requirement: The service must be offered in one language only.
- id: DR-49
  requirement: The service must not claim or guarantee that flights or maintenance meet regulations, and must not include compliance-audit features. The drone histories in DR-11 are records to be shown, not a compliance guarantee.
- id: DR-50
  requirement: The service must not include data-retention or data-deletion features.
- id: DR-51
  requirement: The service must not include backups, high-availability arrangements or operation spread over several servers.
- id: DR-52
  requirement: The service must not include weather information.
- id: DR-53
  requirement: The service must not include billing or pricing of the work.
